heya -

there's no model provided here and also using UUID you haven't indicated what kind of datatype you are using for that; SQLAlchemy doesnt have a built in UUID datatype for MySQL.    Here is an [MCVE](http://stackoverflow.com/help/mcve) using a paraphrased version of [our own GUID recipe](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/core/custom_types.html#backend-agnostic-guid-type) and an equivalent IN operation as you have above and it passes for me, if you can try running this:

```py

import uuid

from sqlalchemy import CHAR
from sqlalchemy import Column
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy import Integer
from sqlalchemy import tuple_
from sqlalchemy import TypeDecorator
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from sqlalchemy.types import CHAR
from sqlalchemy.types import TypeDecorator

class GUID(TypeDecorator):
    impl = CHAR(32)
    cache_ok = True

    def process_bind_param(self, value, dialect):
        if value is None:
            return value
        else:
            if not isinstance(value, uuid.UUID):
                return "%.32x" % uuid.UUID(value).int
            else:
                # hexstring
                return "%.32x" % value.int

    def process_result_value(self, value, dialect):
        if value is None:
            return value
        else:
            if not isinstance(value, uuid.UUID):
                value = uuid.UUID(value)
            return value


Base = declarative_base()


class A(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'a'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(GUID)

e = create_engine("mysql+pymysql://scott:tiger@localhost/test", echo=True)
Base.metadata.drop_all(e)
Base.metadata.create_all(e)

s = Session(e)

u1, u2, u3 = uuid.uuid4(), uuid.uuid4(), uuid.uuid4()

s.add_all([A(id=1, data=u1), A(id=2, data=u2), A(id=3, data=u3)])
s.commit()

obj = s.query(A).filter(
    tuple_(A.id, A.data).in_([(2, u2), (3, u3)])
).all()
print(obj)

# run it again to make sure caching isn't causing a problem
obj = s.query(A).filter(
    tuple_(A.id, A.data).in_([(2, u2), (3, u3)])
).all()
print(obj)
```

Hi @zzzeek, thanks for the example! I was able to adjust it to reproduce my issue, and as a result discovered what was happening:

```python
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy import tuple_
from sqlalchemy import Integer
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy import Column
from sqlalchemy_utils import UUIDType
import uuid


Base = declarative_base()


class A(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'a'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(UUIDType)


e = create_engine("mysql+pymysql://root:password@localhost/test", echo=True)
Base.metadata.drop_all(e)
Base.metadata.create_all(e)

s = Session(e)

u1, u2, u3 = uuid.uuid4(), uuid.uuid4(), uuid.uuid4()

s.add_all([A(id=1, data=u1), A(id=2, data=u2), A(id=3, data=u3)])
s.commit()

my_set = set(s.query(A.id, A.data).filter(A.id == 2))
print(my_set)

# Uncomment to fix:
# my_set = {(x, y) for x, y in my_set}

obj = s.query(A).filter(
    tuple_(A.id, A.data).in_(my_set)
).all()
print(obj)

# run it again to make sure caching isn't causing a problem
obj = s.query(A).filter(
    tuple_(A.id, A.data).in_(my_set)
).all()
print(obj)
```

It seems that the result from a previous query no longer behaves like a tuple when it is used as input to a later query. Luckily this is easy to work around.

here's the MCVE for that

```py
from sqlalchemy import Column
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy import Integer
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy import tuple_
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

Base = declarative_base()


class A(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'a'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(String)

e = create_engine("sqlite://", echo=True)
Base.metadata.create_all(e)

s = Session(e)

u1, u2, u3 = "a", "b", "c"

s.add_all([A(id=1, data=u1), A(id=2, data=u2), A(id=3, data=u3)])
s.commit()


queried_tuples = s.execute(select(A.id, A.data)).all()[1:3]

# uncomment to fix
#queried_tuples = [(x, y) for x, y in queried_tuples]

obj = s.execute(select(A).filter(
    tuple_(A.id, A.data).in_(queried_tuples)
)).all()
print(obj)

```
I guess we do an `isinstance(values[0], tuple)` or something somewhere

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**use tuple expansion if type._is_tuple, test for Sequence if no type** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/3285

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **rel_1_4** branch:

**use tuple expansion if type._is_tuple, test for Sequence if no type** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/3286

> I guess we do an `isinstance(values[0], tuple)` or something somewhere

well there was exactly that code already but the Row isn't tuple, it's Sequence.  i fortunately recalled also that when you do isinstance(Sequence) you have to block out strings and bytes.   But also, where this decision happens, most of the time we know we have TupleType so we now go off that in the default case and only do an isinstance() if it's a plain textual expression with no typing information added.
